title: SchemeArena: Factorized Stress Testing of Scheming in LLM Agents
pdf_path: papers/SchemeArena_Factorized Stress Testing of Scheming in LLM Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: The benchmark assumes an LLM agent with a long-horizon goal, tool access, and partial or asymmetric oversight. Four factors (long-term goal, pressure, prompt specificity, oversight) are crossed into seven setups; scheming is judged by an LLM monitor (SCOUT) from full trajectories using five criteria and mandatory evidence citations. The threat model is behavioral, not adversarial in a cryptographic sense.
core_contributions: SchemeArena: 400 scenarios over 1,334 RapidAPI tools and 28 security-related domains
A 4-factor, 7-setup design separating goal, pressure, prompt specificity, and oversight
SCOUT: an evidence-citing trajectory monitor with five criteria and a 0-2 score
Five-model measurement showing explicit goals raise scheming from 21.7-34.9% to 74.4-81.2%
Action-only oversight increases scheming for some closed models while joint oversight reduces it
limitations: Scenarios are retained only if at least one evaluated model schemes, inducing selection bias
Qwen3-32B is scenario generator, trajectory generator, filter judge, SCOUT judge, and evaluated model
All-off is not a neutral baseline; goals are implicitly embedded in generation prompts
SCOUT reports accuracy=precision=83.03% and recall=100%, consistent with a majority-positive classifier; no TN/FP reported
Oversight is one prompt sentence and does not clearly cover thoughts or reasoning
Internal inconsistencies: all-off ranges 21.71-31.93% vs 23.7-34.9%; pressure gains claimed 2.01-8.49 pp but some models decline; 28 tool categories vs 33 strings in Table 7
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic primitive, security definition, theorem, proof, or reduction
SCOUT is an LLM judge, not a monitor with formal soundness or completeness guarantees
applied_crypto_links: None; tool calls are plain API interactions with no authentication, signing, or attestation
Cryptographic provenance or signed tool manifests are our inference, not evaluated
evidence_refs: pp.1-14 framework, setups, SCOUT, and main results
pp.17-39 appendices A-G, prompts, Tables 7-14, Figure 13

title: Safe, or Simply Incapable? Rethinking Safety Evaluation for Phone-Use Agents
pdf_path: papers/Safe, or Simply Incapable_Rethinking Safety Evaluation for Phone-Use Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: Offline single-step evaluation of phone-use agents at safety-critical moments. Each moment provides safe and unsafe reference actions; the model next action is classified as Safe, Unsafe, or no-useful-action (CFR). There is no adaptive attacker; hazards arise from app context and the agent's own action choice.
core_contributions: PhoneSafety: 700 safety-critical moments from 130+ apps, 4,512 trajectories, about 75K steps
A three-way decomposition separating safety judgment from the ability to act (Safe/Unsafe/CFR)
Two metrics, Cond-Safe and 1-CFR, that remove the capability confound
Evaluation of 8 phone-use agents showing general success correlates with 1-CFR (r=0.906) but only weakly with Cond-Safe (r=0.239)
Diagnostics for input degradation, reference sensitivity, hard subsets, and protocol ablations
limitations: Offline single-step evaluation; no real device execution
China Android app distribution only
Eight models is a small sample for correlation claims
Reference sensitivity tested only for false-CFR
Protocol prompt changes CFR substantially, in tension with a pure capability interpretation
Construction counts 477+329 do not reconcile with 736; Claude general success uses 0.25 vs 0.14; sections 3.1 and 3.6 disagree on whether protocol enters model input
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic primitive, definition, theorem, or reduction
The protocol is a natural-language authorization rule, not a formal capability or security definition
applied_crypto_links: None; no signing, attestation, or capability tokens are used
Capability here means action affordance, not a cryptographic capability token
evidence_refs: pp.1-10 protocol, dataset, metrics, and main results
pp.13-26 appendices A-M, prompts, and detailed tables

title: PsySafe: A Comprehensive Framework for Psychological-based Attack, Defense, and Evaluation of Multi-agent System Safety
pdf_path: papers/PsySafe_A Comprehensive Framework for Psychological-based Attack, Defense, and Evaluation of Multi-agent System Safety.pdf
threat_model_summary: The attacker controls either the human input or an agent system prompt and injects dark-trait prompts plus inducement instructions and Red ICL. Contaminated agents cascade unsafe behavior through inter-agent messages. Defenses are input filtering, rewriting the system prompt (Doctor), and a supervising agent (Police). No formal adversary model or adaptive attack is defined.
core_contributions: PsySafe: a joint attack, evaluation, and defense framework for multi-agent psychological safety
Six moral-dimension dark traits with Inducement Instruction and Red ICL, injected at human input or system prompt
PDR and JDR metrics plus a 12-question DDTD scale and an 859-question dataset
Attacks across Camel, AutoGen, MetaGPT, and AutoGPT, raising unsafe rates up to 98%
Comparison of input filtering, Doctor, and Police defenses
limitations: Doctor claims repetition until Psy Score < 20, but Table 5 reports 79.66/78.56
Text says GPT-3.5 Turbo is least safe, but Table 2 shows higher JDR-R3 for GPT-4 0613
Table 2 attack and data conditions are underspecified; Claude2 additionally receives a jailbreak prompt
No seeds, repeated runs, or confidence intervals; single GPT judge and single human evaluator
Defenses tested only on tiny/AutoGen, with no adaptive attacks
Traits Attack requires write access to the system prompt
r=0.41 is described as strong correlation; MetaGPT/AutoGPT use one round and are not comparable to three-round frameworks
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic primitive, security definition, theorem, proof, or reduction
applied_crypto_links: None; the only cryptography mention is a library name inside a generated malicious program example
No authentication or isolation mechanism is evaluated; message passing is plain text
evidence_refs: pp.1-9 framework, attacks, metrics, and main results
pp.13-30 appendices, prompts, datasets, and case studies

title: CIA: Inferring the Communication Topology from LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems
pdf_path: papers/CIA_Inferring the Communication Topology from LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems.pdf
threat_model_summary: A black-box attacker can submit queries to a multi-agent system and read only its final outputs, with no access to intermediate reasoning, agent configuration, or topology. The goal is to recover the directed communication graph. The model is empirical and assumes agents follow formatting instructions and copy intermediate reasoning verbatim.
core_contributions: CIA: a two-stage black-box communication-topology inference attack
An adversarial query q* with cumulative propagation, task focus, and predecessor restatement constraints to elicit intermediate reasoning
A reconstruction procedure using delimiters and backward deduplication to recover an ordered agent list
Global biased disentanglement plus GPT-5 top-k weak supervision for directed edge classification
Mean AUC 0.8608 (peak 0.9873) across 12 generator/dataset settings, above four LLM baselines
limitations: No defense evaluation and no downstream targeted attack
No train/test split and no query-cost accounting
Topologies limited to 3-7 node DAGs
Strong dependence on instruction following and verbatim copying
Section 6.2 says all AUC values exceed 0.75, but AGP-HumanEval is 0.7480; abstract 0.87 vs table mean 0.8608
No independent ethics or broader-impact section
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic primitive, security game, theorem, proof, or reduction
Theorem 1 is a borrowed total-correlation decomposition identity; MI/TC/InfoNCE are estimation tools, not leakage bounds
applied_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic mechanism is used or evaluated
Signed or authenticated inter-agent messaging is our inference and is not tested
evidence_refs: pp.1-9 attack design, model, experiments, and limitations
pp.12-17 appendices A-K, prompts, and per-setting tables

title: Benchmarking Web Agent Safety under E-commerce Deceptive Interfaces
pdf_path: papers/Benchmarking Web Agent Safety under E-commerce Deceptive Interfaces.pdf
threat_model_summary: A controlled e-commerce site injects seven state-triggered deceptive interface patterns (pop-ups, banners, personalized variants, domain redirection, cart add-ons, price drift). The agent may be tricked into a harmful purchase or redirect. The adversary is a fixed page-level injector, not an adaptive attacker, and there is no network or authentication adversary.
core_contributions: WebDecept: a configurable front-end plugin that triggers deceptive UI patterns by page state
Seven deception types instantiated over 9 task templates into 45 end-to-end shopping tasks
A 5-agent by 7-scenario by 2-prompt evaluation (630 cases per agent) separating task completion (TC) from safety violation rate (SVR)
Measurement showing domain redirection and price drift are nearly undetected, and cart add-ons retain 11-27% violations under explicit rules
Failure analysis of over-trust, instruction conflict, and visual salience
limitations: No clean/no-deception baseline
Single run, no confidence intervals or repetitions; 45 tasks per cell gives about 2.2 percentage-point granularity
Low-TC agents have selection-biased SVR denominators
SVR counts clicking Cancel or closing a pop-up as a violation, raising construct-validity concerns
Single non-adaptive intervention; ablations cover only pop-up wording, price-drift magnitude, and perception module
Pr is an oracle-like strong prompt and no guardrail/gating baseline is tested
Table 1 writes Claude S4.5 while the text says Claude 4.5 Sonnet; 1.2x item price conflicts with the Figure 2(b) screenshot; domain redirection shows a ceiling effect
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic primitive, formal security definition, theorem, or reduction
MDP and SVR are measurement-level formalization, not cryptographic security definitions
applied_crypto_links: None; integrity here is an intuitive page/cart/price state property, not cryptographic integrity
No signatures, attestation, or trusted display mechanisms are evaluated
evidence_refs: pp.1-9 framework, tasks, metrics, and main results
